newsitem.title: DUBAI: Dubai police pursue bid to control Internet.
newsitem.headline: Dubai police pursue bid to control Internet.

text.p: Dubai's police chief has said he has not lost hope in his drive to regulate access to the Internet in the UAE, underlining concern over the computer web in the conservative Gulf region where publications are censored.
Newspapers on Tuesday said Major General Dhahi Khalfan Tamim made his comments at a seminar on how to monitor the Internet.

"When told that putting water-tight restrictions on access to the Internet is impossible, we did not lose hope, especially since we came to know that Singapore has successfully done it. In the world of computer programming we believe nothing is beyond reach," the Khaleej Times quoted him as saying.

The Gulf News quoted Tamim as saying that when Dubai police voiced concern about the need to control access to the Internet "the answer was always the same. We were told any attempt to control the use of the Internet is a waste of time."

Singapore government measures to regulate political and religious content on the Internet and keep it free of pornography became effective in July last year. They require all Internet service operators and local content providers to be registered with the Singapore Broadcasting Authority. Failure to heed the measures can result in a fine or licence cancellation.

Tamim last year entered a rare public row in the United Arab Emirates saying the information ministry and the police, rather than the telecommunications company Etisalat, which provides Internet access, should be authorised to issue Internet licences as it was their job to monitor information coming into the UAE and maintain security.
The UAE, where newspapers, magazines, books and films are censored, is anxious about the spread of pornography and political material over web sites.

Etisalat had said it would disconnect any customers who abused Internet serivces and violated "order and clear laws" of the UAE, where official figures show that the number of Internet subscribers rose to 9,669 in 1996 from 2,503 in 1995.
